title: Prophylaxis and Empirical Therapy in Cancer Patients

questions.stem: A 42-year-old man was brought in by ambulance with sudden onset fever and collapse. He was known to have acute myeloid leukemia and had received induction chemotherapy 10 days earlier. He was taking levofloxacin prophylaxis. On examination his temperature was 38.5°C, his heart rate was 110 beats/minute, and his blood pressure was 84/42 mmHg. He was peripherally vasodilated. He had widespread inspiratory crackles on chest auscultation and mucositis on oral examination. Investigations: Neutrophil count 0.0 ×109/L CXR: diffuse infiltrates bilaterally Blood cultures: gram-positive cocci after 11 hours
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.explanation: Viridans group streptococci Viridans group streptococci have been well described as virulent pathogens in neutropenic patients. The source of bacteremia is typically from the upper GI track, and often patients will have significant mucositis. It can cause a GNR-like sepsis picture clinically as well as acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Breakthrough infections on fluoroquinolone prophylaxis can occur, especially with ciprofloxacin due to the poor antistreptococcal activity.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q39

questions.question: A patient with acute myeloid leukemia and deteriorating respiratory distress.
questions.question_raw: A patient with AML with deteriorating respiratory distress.

parts.text: What agent would you use to manage aspergillosis?
What risk factors put a patient at highest risk for a mould infection?

parts_raw.text: What agent would you use to manage aspergillosis?
What risk factors will make a patient at highest risk for a mould infection?

questions.model_answer:
a) Voriconazole is the recommended primary therapy for invasive aspergillosis (superior survival vs amphotericin B deoxycholate in the pivotal randomized trial); liposomal amphotericin B or isavuconazole are alternatives.
b) (1) Prolonged and profound neutropenia (highest risk, e.g. after AML induction chemotherapy). (2) High-dose corticosteroids and/or acute or chronic GVHD after HSCT. (3) Other profound immune defects – chronic granulomatous disease, AIDS, lung/solid-organ transplantation.

cohort_answer.text: Voriconazole. || Prolonged neutropenia, prolonged antibiotic exposure, CGD.

questions.question: In patients with high-risk neutropenia, describe the advantages and disadvantages of preemptive (diagnostic-driven) antifungal prophylaxis compared with empirical antifungal therapy for invasive fungal infection.

parts.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts_raw.text: In patients with high risk neutropenia, describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

questions.model_answer: a) Advantages: (1) Substantially reduced antifungal exposure/overtreatment, since the empirical approach treats a single symptom (fever) and results in large-scale unnecessary antifungal use, whereas the diagnostic-driven approach treats only when highly suggestive criteria (galactomannan, CT findings, culture) are present. (2) Consequent reduction in drug toxicity, cost, and selection pressure for resistant fungi, without an increase in mortality versus empirical therapy. Disadvantages: (1) It detects/diagnoses MORE invasive fungal infections (the preemptive arm consistently identifies more IFD, reflecting delayed or missed early treatment of subclinical disease), and non-inferiority for survival was not clearly demonstrated in the highest-risk first-induction subgroup. (2) It requires resource-intensive infrastructure: a readily available thin-slice chest CT with skilled radiologists, reliable galactomannan/antigen assays with a turnaround of 2-3 days, and mold-active prophylaxis reduces galactomannan sensitivity/specificity, lowering the test's reliability.

cohort_answer.text: Advantages: antifungal sparing (reducing risk of resistance); sparing from adverse events associated with prophylaxis (liver tox, rashes, reactions). Disadvantages: requires patient compliance for ongoing routine bloodwork; requires available access to a consistent laboratory for testing; high risk patients may develop disease in between testing

questions.question: List indications for adding or including vancomycin in the empirical regimen for a patient with febrile neutropenia.

parts.text: List four indications for adding or including vancomycin in the empiric regimen for a patient with febrile neutropenia.

parts_raw.text: List FOUR indications for adding or including vancomycin in empiric regimen for patient with febrile neutropenia

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Hemodynamic instability / septic shock (empirical therapy should then add gram-positive cover). (2) Suspected central venous catheter-related infection (e.g., fever with signs at the catheter site, or fever concurrent with line flushing). (3) Clinically suspected pneumonia. (4) Isolation of, or known colonization with, a resistant gram-positive pathogen requiring glycopeptide cover — MRSA (or methicillin-resistant S. epidermidis), penicillin-resistant pneumococcus, or resistant enterococcus — or care in a center with a high incidence of such infections. (Skin/soft-tissue infection due to gram-positive cocci is an additional standard indication.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The skin/soft-tissue infection indication and the formal enumerated list are from the IDSA 2010 febrile neutropenia guideline.

questions.question: A patient has febrile neutropenia. Aside from MRSA colonization, list indications for empirical treatment with vancomycin (gram-positive-directed therapy).

parts.text: Aside from MRSA colonization, list four indications for empiric treatment with vancomycin.

parts_raw.text: Aside from MRSA colonization list 4 indications for empiric treatment

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Hemodynamic instability / septic shock. (2) Suspected central venous catheter-related infection (catheter-site signs, or fever developing with line flushing). (3) Clinically suspected pneumonia. (4) Isolation of a penicillin-resistant pneumococcus or a resistant enterococcus (or another gram-positive organism suggesting a gram-positive etiology). (Skin/soft-tissue infection is a further standard indication.)
questions.beyond_mandell: The skin/soft-tissue infection indication is from the IDSA 2010 febrile neutropenia guideline.

Diagnostic tests of choice. Treatment of choice.

The kid dies, and the ICU is upset he died of invasive aspergillus, and wants to know about Posaconazole prophylaxis. What is the most important factor to consider before using posaconazole prophylaxis.

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Prior/concurrent anti-mould therapy – decreases sensitivity. (2) BAL versus serum sample – BAL gives higher sensitivity than serum. (3) Piperacillin-tazobactam/other antibiotics (or Bifidobacterium in neonates) – false positives, decreasing specificity.
b) Diagnostics: chest CT plus bronchoscopy/BAL for culture and cytology, with serum and/or BAL galactomannan (tissue biopsy for definitive/proven diagnosis). Treatment: voriconazole (liposomal amphotericin B if voriconazole contraindicated), with reduction of immunosuppression.
c) Whether the patient is genuinely at high risk for invasive aspergillosis – posaconazole prophylaxis is guideline-recommended specifically for AML/MDS patients with prolonged neutropenia from chemotherapy and for allogeneic HSCT recipients with GVHD (also weigh adequate drug absorption/levels and interactions, and its more serious adverse events).

cohort_answer.text: Decrease sensitivity: CGD/Job syndrome; concomitant antifungal use; serum sample source. Decrease specificity: PipTazo and AmoxClav; other fungi (Penicillium, fusarium, histo); chemo (gut translocation from mucositis); COPD (colonization). Diagnostic tests: Tissue specimen for culture/histopathology/cytology; fluid; serum/BAL galactomannan; CT scan; PJP/legionella PCR; mycoplasma culture. Treatment: Empiric PipTazo/Vanco; Amphotericin B liposomal; reduce immunosuppression if possible. Posaconazole prophylaxis consideration: underlying disease state - recommend prophylaxis with posaconazole, voriconazole, and/or micafungin during prolonged neutropenia for high-risk IA patients (hematologic disorders with poorly functioning neutrophils, acute leukemia with repeated/prolonged neutropenia, prior IA before transplant); posaconazole recommended for allogeneic HSCT recipients with GVHD at high risk for IA; systemic triazole or inhaled AmB for 3-4 months after lung transplant. 3 indications for posaconazole prophylaxis shown to reduce mortality in trials: severe GVHD; primary prophylaxis in AML undergoing chemo; primary prophylaxis in MDS undergoing chemo.

questions.question: A cancer patient has fever with no obvious source clinically or radiographically. The patient is on piperacillin-tazobactam. The central venous line and peripheral lines are now growing a yeast-like organism.
questions.question_raw: Cancer patient with fever and no obvious source clinically or radiographically. On PipTazo. CVL and peripheral lines now growing a yeast-like organism.

parts.text: What is the source of the fever?
Name 4 other potential sources of fever.

parts_raw.text: What is the source of the fever?
Name 4 other potential sources of fever

questions.model_answer:
a) Candidemia (invasive candidiasis), most likely catheter-associated (about 80% of candidemias occur in patients with a venous catheter as the likely source), though gut translocation across chemotherapy-damaged mucosa is an alternative source in this cancer patient.
b) (1) Repeat blood cultures from all lumens and a peripheral vein to confirm and follow clearance, with species identification (germ tube test/MALDI-TOF) and susceptibilities. (2) Dilated funduscopic ophthalmology examination in every candidemic patient to detect ocular candidiasis. (3) Echocardiography (transesophageal if persistently positive) for endocarditis, plus abdominal imaging if a deep source is suspected.
c) (1) Other bacterial infection/abscess. (2) Other fungal infection. (3) Viral infection. (4) Non-infectious causes such as the underlying malignancy, drug fever, or thrombosis.
d) (1) Start an echinocandin (caspofungin, micafungin, or anidulafungin) as first-line therapy. (2) Remove/replace the central venous catheter. (3) Step down to fluconazole once the isolate is fluconazole-susceptible, blood cultures have cleared, and the patient is stable. (4) Lipid-formulation amphotericin B as an alternative if intolerant/resistant. (Voriconazole is an option when added mold coverage is desired.)

cohort_answer.text: A) Fungemia - line associated or gut translocation (candidemia often from gut translocation rather than line, so don't always change lines if repeat culture negative). B) Repeat blood cultures from all lines; if Candida spp -> germ tube test; if Candida -> ophtho consult; abdominal imaging if source unclear; echocardiogram especially if persistently positive cultures. C) Infectious - bacterial (including abscess), viral, other fungal infection; Non-infectious - cancer, thrombosis, drug. D) Remove CVC; empiric echinocandin; stop PipTazo if not neutropenic; reduce immunosuppression if feasible. (IDSA alternatives: echinocandin, lipid formulation AmB 3-5mg/kg daily, fluconazole 800mg loading then 400mg daily, voriconazole 400mg BID x2 doses then 200-300mg BID.)

questions.question: A patient with febrile neutropenia is shown a picture of ecthyma gangrenosum. [image-based question: ecthyma gangrenosum]
questions.question_raw: Patient with febrile neutropenia, shown a picture of ecthyma gangrenosum.

parts.text: Give two possible diagnoses (one to species level, one to genus level).
State the empiric antimicrobial treatment pending further investigations.

parts_raw.text: Two possible diagnoses (one to species level, one to genus level).
Empiric antimicrobial tx pending further investigations?

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Species level: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (ecthyma gangrenosum is its characteristic manifestation of bacteremia in neutropenic hosts). (2) Genus level: Aspergillus species (ecthyma-like lesions can also be caused by other gram-negatives, fungi such as Aspergillus/Fusarium, and viruses). b) Empiric broad-spectrum antipseudomonal beta-lactam - piperacillin-tazobactam, cefepime, or meropenem - as monotherapy per febrile-neutropenia guidance; add a second antipseudomonal agent (aminoglycoside or antipseudomonal fluoroquinolone) if critically ill or high local resistance, and add vancomycin if hemodynamically unstable or MRSA/skin involvement, with treatment of the bacteremia and local wound care.
questions.beyond_mandell: The empiric febrile-neutropenia regimen (monotherapy plus escalation criteria, addition of vancomycin) derives from IDSA febrile-neutropenia guidance rather than this chapter, which describes antipseudomonal therapy generally.

cohort_answer.text: A) Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staph aureus, Strep pyogenes; fungal: Candida albicans, Mucor, Aspergillus, Fusarium. B) PipTazo (antipseudomonal) or Meropenem; double cover with aminoglycoside if critically ill; add anti-MRSA agent (Vanco) if critically ill.

questions.question: In patients with high-risk neutropenia, describe the advantages and disadvantages of preemptive (diagnostic-driven) antifungal prophylaxis compared with empirical antifungal therapy for invasive fungal infection.
questions.question_raw: 26. In patients with high risk neutropenia, describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

parts_raw.text: Describe two advantages and two disadvantages of preemptive prophylaxis over empiric prophylaxis for invasive fungal infection.

questions.model_answer: a) Advantages: (1) Less antifungal drug use, avoiding the marked overtreatment inherent in empirical therapy (which treats fever alone), with reduced cost, lower toxicity, and less selection pressure for resistant fungi. (2) No increase in overall mortality compared with the empirical approach, so IFD outcomes are not compromised by the more restrained strategy. Disadvantages: (1) More invasive fungal infections are detected/occur in the diagnostic-driven arm, and non-inferiority for survival was not demonstrated in the highest-risk first-remission-induction subgroup. (2) It depends on resource-heavy diagnostics: readily available thin-slice chest CT with skilled radiologists, reliable galactomannan/antigen assays with 2-3 day turnaround, and its reliability falls when mold-active prophylaxis lowers galactomannan sensitivity/specificity.

cohort_answer.text: Pre-emptive often involves serial HRCT and Galactomannan/B-D-Glucan. Advantages: Decreased costs of antifungal drugs; lower risk of resistance; minimises risk of drug related toxicity. Disadvantages: Requires frequent testing; delayed start of therapy; higher rates of invasive fungal infection.
